q: What is MLOps and how does it differ from DevOps?
a: MLOps applies DevOps principles, automation, version control, testing, continuous delivery and monitoring, to machine learning systems, but ML adds assets and failure modes that ordinary software does not have. In addition to code, you must version data, features, models and experiments, because a model is the product of code plus data. Testing includes data validation and model evaluation, not just unit tests, since a pipeline can run successfully and still produce a worse model. Deployment includes model registries, staged rollouts and rollback. Monitoring covers not only latency and errors but also data drift, prediction quality and fairness, because performance can decay silently as the world changes. Retraining pipelines, triggered by schedule, drift or new data, close the loop. As a platform engineer, I provide the shared infrastructure for these steps: pipelines, registries, feature stores, compute and observability.
f: What is data drift?
Which artefacts need versioning in ML?
p: MLOps adds data, features, models and experiments to the versioned assets, data and model validation to testing, and drift and quality to monitoring, with retraining pipelines closing the loop.
cmds: dvc add data/train.parquet && git add data/train.parquet.dvc
tip: Say the new failure mode is silent quality decay.

q: What does a production ML pipeline look like, from data to deployed model?
a: A typical pipeline has stages that are automated and reproducible. Data ingestion pulls from sources into a versioned dataset, followed by validation that checks schema, ranges, missing values and drift against expectations. Feature engineering transforms raw data, ideally with the same code used at serving time, often through a feature store. Training runs on scalable compute with tracked parameters and seeds, and produces a model artefact. Evaluation compares the candidate against a baseline on held-out data and fairness or safety slices, with thresholds that gate promotion. The approved model is registered with its metadata, lineage and metrics, then deployed through a staged process, shadow or canary, to a serving platform. Monitoring tracks inference quality, latency and drift, and triggers retraining when needed. The orchestration is handled by tools such as Kubeflow Pipelines, Argo Workflows or Airflow, with everything defined as code and run in CI.
f: Why must feature code be shared between training and serving?
Which stages gate promotion?
p: Ingest and validate data, build features shared with serving, train with tracked parameters, evaluate against a baseline with gating thresholds, register, deploy gradually and monitor, with an orchestrator running it all as code.
tip: Stress validation and evaluation gates; they are the ML-specific parts.

q: What is training-serving skew and how do you prevent it?
a: Training-serving skew means the model sees different data or features in production than it saw during training, so its accuracy falls even though the model file is unchanged. Causes include different code paths for computing features offline and online, different handling of missing values, time zones or units, data leakage in training that is impossible at serving time, stale features, and changes in upstream data schemas. Prevention starts with using the same feature definitions and code for both, which is the main purpose of a feature store with an offline and an online store. Point-in-time correct joins avoid using future information in training. I log the features actually served and compare their distributions with the training data, alerting on drift or schema changes, and I validate inputs at the serving boundary. Integration tests that run the same examples through both paths, and shadow deployments, catch remaining differences before users are affected.
f: What is point-in-time correctness?
How do you detect skew in production?
p: Skew arises when production features differ from training features. Share feature definitions through a feature store, use point-in-time joins, log served features and compare distributions, validate inputs and test both paths with identical examples.
tip: Say one definition of each feature, used in both paths.

q: What is a feature store and when do you need one?
a: A feature store is a system that manages the definition, computation, storage and serving of features for ML. It has an offline store, holding historical feature values for training, often in a data warehouse or lake, and an online store, a low-latency key-value database for real-time inference, kept consistent with each other. It provides a registry so teams can discover and reuse features, point-in-time joins to avoid leakage, and monitoring of freshness and quality. You need one when multiple models or teams reuse the same features, when you serve real-time predictions that need consistent online and offline values, or when training-serving skew causes problems. For a single batch model with a few features, it is overkill, and a well-organised pipeline is enough. Options include Feast, Tecton, and the feature stores built into cloud platforms. The cost is another system to operate, so adopt it when the reuse and consistency benefits are real.
f: What is the difference between online and offline stores?
When is it overkill?
p: A feature store provides a registry, offline storage for training, online storage for low-latency serving, point-in-time joins and freshness monitoring. Adopt it for reuse across models and real-time consistency; skip it for a single simple batch model.
tip: Say it is justified by reuse and online-offline consistency.

q: How do you use a model registry and track experiments?
a: Experiment tracking records, for every training run, the code version, data version, hyperparameters, metrics, plots and artefacts, so any result can be reproduced and compared. Tools like MLflow, Weights and Biases or cloud-native equivalents provide this. A model registry then manages the lifecycle of models that are worth keeping: each registered model has versions, lineage back to the run and data, metrics, a description, and stages or aliases such as staging and production. Promotion from one stage to the next is a controlled action, gated by automated evaluation and sometimes human approval, and the deployment system pulls by alias, so rollback is just pointing the alias at a previous version. I add access control, audit logs and signed or checksummed artefacts so that what runs in production is exactly what was approved. This gives traceability, which regulators and incident reviews often require.
f: What lineage should a registered model have?
How does rollback work with aliases?
p: Track runs with code, data, parameters and metrics for reproducibility, and use a registry with versions, lineage, aliases and gated promotion. Deploy by alias so rollback is repointing, with access control and audit.
tip: Emphasise lineage and alias-based rollback.

q: How do you detect and respond to data drift and concept drift?
a: Data drift means the distribution of input features changes from the training data, for example a new customer segment or a changed sensor. Concept drift means the relationship between inputs and the target changes, so the same inputs now imply a different outcome. To detect data drift, I compare production feature distributions with a reference window using statistical measures such as population stability index, Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests or divergence measures, per feature, with alert thresholds tuned to avoid noise. Concept drift shows up as degrading performance, which needs ground-truth labels that may arrive late, so I track proxy metrics and delayed accuracy when labels become available. Responses depend on severity: investigate upstream data issues first, since many drift alerts are really pipeline bugs, then retrain on recent data, adjust thresholds, or fall back to a simpler model. Automating retraining with validation gates helps, but a human should review significant changes.
f: Why do labels often arrive late?
Which drift alerts are really pipeline bugs?
p: Compare production feature distributions with a reference using PSI or statistical tests for data drift, and watch delayed accuracy and proxies for concept drift. Check upstream pipelines first, then retrain with gated validation.
tip: Say many drift alerts turn out to be upstream data bugs.

q: How do you reproduce a model training run months later?
a: Reproducibility needs every input captured. The code is pinned by Git commit. Data is versioned, with tools like DVC or lakehouse table snapshots, or immutable dated partitions, so I can retrieve exactly the training set. Environment is captured with a container image built from pinned dependencies and recorded by digest, with the CUDA and driver versions noted. Configuration and hyperparameters are stored in files or the tracking system, and random seeds are set and logged. Non-determinism from GPUs and parallelism can still cause small differences, so I record whether deterministic modes were used, and accept small numerical variation. The experiment tracker links all of these to the resulting artefact in the registry. I test reproducibility periodically by re-running an old job and comparing the metrics within a tolerance, because untested reproducibility is usually broken in some detail.
f: Why can GPU training be non-deterministic?
How do you version large datasets?
p: Pin code by commit, version data with DVC or table snapshots, capture the environment by container digest and driver versions, log configuration and seeds, link everything in the tracker, and periodically re-run to verify.
cmds: docker run --rm registry/train@sha256:abc123 python train.py --config cfg.yaml --seed 42
tip: Say you actually re-run an old job to test reproducibility.

q: Compare batch, real-time and streaming inference patterns.
a: Batch inference runs the model over a large dataset on a schedule, writing predictions to a store, for example nightly recommendations or risk scores. It is the simplest and cheapest, with no latency requirement, and it uses compute efficiently, but predictions can be stale. Real-time or online inference serves predictions per request over an API with tight latency, perhaps tens to hundreds of milliseconds, which needs always-on, autoscaled serving, online feature retrieval and careful monitoring, and is more expensive and complex. Streaming inference processes events continuously, for example fraud scoring on a transaction stream, combining windowed features with a model, and sits between the two. I choose by freshness needs: if predictions can be a few hours old, batch is far simpler. Many systems mix them, precomputing most results in batch and calling real-time inference only where fresh context matters.
f: When would you precompute and cache predictions?
What makes online serving harder to operate?
p: Batch is simple and cheap but stale, real-time serves per request with strict latency and higher cost, and streaming scores events continuously. Choose by freshness need and often combine batch with selective real-time.
tip: Ask how fresh predictions need to be before choosing.

q: What is KServe and how does it help serve models on Kubernetes?
a: KServe is a Kubernetes-native model serving platform. You declare an InferenceService custom resource that points to a model and a runtime, and KServe creates the deployment, networking, autoscaling and routing. It supports standard predictors for frameworks such as scikit-learn, XGBoost, PyTorch and TensorFlow, and runtimes for LLMs, such as vLLM and Hugging Face servers, behind a consistent inference protocol. Key features include autoscaling with Knative, including scale to zero for idle models, canary rollouts by splitting traffic between revisions, transformers for pre and post processing, explainers, model monitoring hooks, and ModelMesh for high-density serving of many small models. For a platform team it standardises how models are deployed, so data scientists need not write Kubernetes manifests, while the platform controls security, quotas and observability. The trade-offs are the additional components such as Knative or Istio, and a learning curve for troubleshooting.
f: What does scale to zero cost you?
How does canary rollout work in KServe?
p: KServe turns an InferenceService resource into a managed deployment with autoscaling, canary traffic splitting, pre and post processing and many runtimes including LLM servers, standardising model serving on Kubernetes.
tip: Mention scale to zero and the cold-start trade-off.

q: How do you orchestrate ML workflows with Kubeflow Pipelines, Argo or Airflow?
a: These tools define a workflow as a graph of steps with dependencies, run them on a schedule or trigger, retry failures and record the history. Kubeflow Pipelines is ML-specific: each step is a containerised component with typed inputs and outputs, artefact and metadata tracking, and caching of unchanged steps. Argo Workflows is a general Kubernetes-native engine in which each step is a pod, well suited for parallel fan-out jobs and CI-like flows. Airflow is a mature scheduler for data pipelines, strong for scheduled ETL with a large operator ecosystem, and is often used to trigger ML jobs. I choose based on existing skills and needs: Kubeflow or Argo if the team is Kubernetes-centric and wants container-native steps, Airflow if the organisation already runs it for data engineering. Whichever I choose, steps are idempotent, parameterised, resource-limited, and the pipeline definitions live in Git and go through review.
f: Why make steps idempotent?
What does step caching save?
p: Kubeflow Pipelines offers typed ML components with artefact tracking and caching, Argo is a general Kubernetes-native DAG engine, Airflow is a mature data scheduler. Choose by existing skills; keep steps idempotent and definitions in Git.
tip: Say the choice follows existing skills, not fashion.

q: How do you apply CI/CD to machine learning, including what gets tested?
a: I extend normal CI with ML-specific checks. On every pull request: linting and unit tests of data and feature code, schema and data validation tests on sample data, and a quick training smoke test on a small dataset to ensure the pipeline runs end to end. For significant changes, a full or scheduled training run produces a candidate model, which is evaluated automatically against a baseline on held-out data, with thresholds for accuracy, latency, fairness slices and size, and failing any threshold blocks promotion. Continuous delivery then packages the model and serving code into a versioned image, deploys it to staging, runs integration and load tests, then performs a canary rollout in production with automatic rollback on monitored metrics. Continuous training pipelines retrain on a schedule or on drift, using the same gates. Everything is reproducible, with data and model versions recorded in the release metadata.
f: What is a smoke test for training?
Which thresholds block promotion?
p: PR checks run unit tests, data validation and a training smoke test; candidate models are evaluated against baselines with gating thresholds; delivery uses staging, load tests and canary with rollback; retraining uses the same gates.
tip: Name the evaluation gate; it replaces 'tests pass' for models.

q: How do you manage data quality and validate data in ML pipelines?
a: Poor data silently produces poor models, so I validate at pipeline boundaries. Schema checks confirm columns, types and nullability. Statistical checks verify ranges, distributions, uniqueness, cardinality and freshness against expectations or recent history. Referential and business rules catch impossible values, for instance negative ages. Tools such as Great Expectations, Pandera, TFX Data Validation or Soda express these as tests. Failures can block the pipeline, quarantine bad records, or alert, depending on severity. I also monitor labels for leakage and imbalance, and check training and serving data for skew. Data contracts agreed with upstream producers make schema changes visible before they break consumers. Findings are logged and linked to model versions, so when a model misbehaves I can look at the exact data quality at training time. Treat data tests as seriously as code tests.
f: What is a data contract?
When should bad data block the pipeline?
p: Validate schema, distributions, freshness and business rules at pipeline boundaries with tools like Great Expectations, block or quarantine on failures, agree data contracts with producers, and log results with model versions.
tip: Say data tests deserve the same seriousness as code tests.

q: What is LLMOps and how does it differ from classical MLOps?
a: LLMOps adapts MLOps to applications built on large language models, where you usually consume a pre-trained model rather than train one from scratch. The central assets change: prompts, retrieval indexes, tool definitions and guardrail configurations replace much of the feature and training pipeline, and you version them like code. Evaluation is harder because outputs are open-ended text, so you rely on curated evaluation sets, rubric grading, LLM judges calibrated with human review, and online feedback. Cost is token-driven and varies per request, so metering and budgets are essential. Latency has new dimensions such as time to first token. Risks are different as well: hallucination, prompt injection, data leakage and unsafe content need guardrails and red teaming. Monitoring includes traces of chains and agents, quality signals and token usage. Fine-tuning, when used, is a smaller part, often with LoRA, and model providers update models underneath you, so pinning and regression testing matter.
f: Which assets does LLMOps version?
Why do provider-side model updates matter?
p: LLMOps versions prompts, indexes and tool definitions, evaluates open-ended output with curated sets and judges, meters tokens, adds guardrails and traces, and handles provider model updates through pinning and regression tests.
tip: Name the new assets: prompts, indexes, tools, guardrails.

q: How do you handle model and data governance, lineage and auditability?
a: Governance is the ability to answer who trained what, on which data, for what purpose, and who approved it. I capture lineage automatically in the pipeline: dataset versions and sources, code commit, parameters, environment, evaluation results and the approver, stored with each registered model. Access control limits who can read sensitive data, run training, promote models and deploy, with audit logs of those actions. Data governance covers consent, retention and deletion, personal data handling and licensing of training data, so a deletion request can be traced to the models affected. Model documentation, such as model cards, describes intended use, limitations, evaluation including fairness slices, and known risks. High-risk systems need human review, impact assessments and monitoring plans, aligned with frameworks like the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and regulations that apply, such as the EU AI Act. The platform's role is to make these records automatic.
f: What does a model card contain?
How would you trace a deletion request to models?
p: Capture lineage automatically in the pipeline, enforce access control and audit logs, manage consent and retention, publish model cards, and align high-risk systems with frameworks such as NIST AI RMF and relevant regulation.
tip: Say the platform should make governance records automatic.

q: How do you control and cache costs of ML training jobs on Kubernetes?
a: I combine scheduling, infrastructure and engineering practices. For compute: use spot or preemptible instances for fault-tolerant training with frequent checkpoints and automatic resume, right-size GPU requests, use queueing with fair share so GPUs do not sit idle, and shut down idle notebooks. For efficiency: mixed precision, efficient data loading, early stopping and hyperparameter search strategies like Bayesian optimisation instead of exhaustive grids. For repeated work: cache pipeline steps whose inputs did not change, reuse preprocessed datasets and pre-trained checkpoints, and avoid re-downloading data and images with node-level caches. For visibility: tag jobs with team and project, measure cost per experiment and per training run, set quotas and budgets, and report to teams. The cheapest training run is the one you do not need to repeat, so reproducibility and caching are also cost controls.
f: How do checkpoints enable spot usage?
What does step caching skip?
p: Use spot with checkpoints, right-size GPUs, queue and fair-share, efficient training practices, cached pipeline steps and datasets, and per-team cost tags and budgets. Reproducibility and caching are cost controls.
tip: Link reproducibility to cost: avoid repeating work.

q: How do you build an evaluation set for an LLM application?
a: I start from real use. I collect representative inputs from production logs, support tickets, or domain experts, covering common requests, edge cases, ambiguous questions, adversarial prompts, and known past failures. For each, I define what a good output means: a reference answer, a set of required facts, a schema, a rubric, or a pass or fail check in code. I get subject matter experts to label a sample, and agree on grading guidelines so different reviewers are consistent. The set is split by category so I can see where the system is weak, and I keep a frozen set for regression and a growing one fed by production failures. Size depends on the variance and importance, but even a hundred well-chosen cases beat anecdotes. I version the set, avoid leaking it into prompts or fine-tuning data, and refresh it as the product evolves, because stale tests give false comfort.
f: How do you avoid leakage into prompts?
How big should an evaluation set be?
p: Collect real inputs including edge and adversarial cases and past failures, define expected outputs or rubrics with expert agreement, slice by category, version it, keep it out of training and prompts, and grow it from production failures.
tip: Say you feed production failures back into the set.

q: What are LLM-as-a-judge evaluations and what are their pitfalls?
a: LLM-as-a-judge uses a strong model to grade the outputs of another model against a rubric, for example scoring helpfulness, faithfulness to sources or following a style guide. It scales far beyond human review and is useful for open-ended outputs where exact matching fails. The pitfalls are real. Judges show biases: preference for longer answers, for their own style or model family, position bias when comparing two answers, and sensitivity to prompt wording. They can be wrong or inconsistent, and may miss subtle factual errors. I mitigate by using clear, specific rubrics with examples, requiring reasoning before a score, randomising answer order in pairwise comparisons, using a different, strong model family as judge, and calibrating against human-labelled samples to measure agreement. I use judge scores as a signal alongside programmatic checks, and I periodically audit them, rather than treating them as ground truth.
f: What is position bias?
How do you measure judge agreement with humans?
p: A strong model grades outputs against a rubric, scaling review but with bias toward length and style, position effects and inconsistency. Use specific rubrics, randomised order, a different judge family, calibration against human labels and audits.
tip: Say you calibrate the judge against human labels.

q: Which metrics do you use to evaluate generation quality beyond accuracy?
a: It depends on the task, but I group them. Correctness: exact match or F1 for extraction, pass rate of unit tests for code, accuracy for classification, and factual consistency scores. Faithfulness or groundedness for RAG, meaning every claim is supported by the supplied context. Relevance and completeness: does the answer address the question fully. Format validity: percentage of outputs that parse against the schema. Safety: toxicity, policy violations, leakage of personal data, and refusal rates, both over-refusal and under-refusal. Style and tone adherence. Operational metrics: latency, tokens and cost per request. User-level metrics: thumbs up and down, edits made by users, task completion and escalation rates. Overlap metrics such as BLEU or ROUGE are weak for open-ended text and I use them only as rough signals. I report a balanced scorecard, because optimising one number can harm another.
f: Why are BLEU and ROUGE weak for LLM outputs?
What is over-refusal?
p: Combine task correctness, faithfulness, relevance, format validity, safety including over-refusal, style, operational cost and latency, and user-level signals. Avoid optimising a single number.
cmds: python metrics.py --pred out.jsonl --gold gold.jsonl --metrics f1 schema_valid faithfulness
tip: Present a scorecard, not a single metric.

q: How do you run online evaluation, A/B tests and monitor quality in production for LLM apps?
a: Offline tests are necessary but not sufficient, because real users behave differently. For online evaluation, I log traces with the prompt version, model, retrieved context and output, with privacy controls. I collect explicit feedback, such as thumbs and comments, and implicit signals like regenerations, edits, copy actions, abandonment and escalation to a human. I sample production traffic for automated scoring by an LLM judge and for periodic human review, and I alert on drops. For changes, I run A/B tests or interleaving between prompt or model variants, with predefined primary metrics and guardrail metrics for cost, latency and safety, and enough traffic to reach statistical significance, taking care with novelty effects. Findings flow back into the evaluation set. I also monitor drift in the input distribution, since new topics can expose gaps, and keep a rollback ready for any variant.
f: What are guardrail metrics in an A/B test?
How do you sample for human review?
p: Log traces with versions, gather explicit and implicit feedback, score sampled traffic with judges and humans, A/B test variants with primary and guardrail metrics, and feed findings back into the evaluation set.
tip: Mention guardrail metrics so an A/B win does not hide a cost or safety loss.

q: How do you red team an LLM application?
a: Red teaming is structured adversarial testing to find failures before attackers or users do. I define the scope and threat model: what harms matter, such as data leakage, policy-violating content, unauthorised actions through tools, and brand damage. Then I generate attacks across categories: direct and indirect prompt injection, jailbreaks, requests for secrets or system prompts, attempts to access other users' data, harmful or biased content, and abuse of tools, with both manual creativity from experts and automated tools like garak or PyRIT that produce many variants. I run them against the full application, including retrieval and tools, not just the bare model, record successes with severity, and fix through layered mitigations: prompt changes, input and output filters, permission reductions, and monitoring. Successful attacks become regression tests. I repeat red teaming on every significant change and periodically, because new attack techniques keep appearing.
f: Why test the full application and not only the model?
How do successful attacks become regression tests?
p: Define threat model and harms, attack with manual and automated techniques across injection, jailbreak, leakage and tool abuse, test the whole application, fix with layered mitigations, and add successes as regression tests; repeat regularly.
tip: Say attacks become regression tests.

q: How do you benchmark an inference service for latency and throughput?
a: I replicate real traffic as closely as I can. First I characterise the workload from production logs: the distribution of prompt lengths and output lengths, request arrival pattern, concurrency, and share of cached prefixes. Then I use a load generator that replays or samples that distribution, with open-loop arrivals at target rates, not only closed-loop fixed concurrency, because real users do not wait for each other. I increase the request rate in steps and record time to first token, inter-token latency, end-to-end latency percentiles at p50, p95 and p99, throughput in tokens per second, error rate, and GPU metrics. The key result is the saturation point: the highest rate at which latency still meets the SLO. I run long enough to include warm-up and steady state, repeat for each configuration, such as quantisation or batch limits, and document hardware and software versions so results are comparable and reproducible.
f: Why use open-loop load?
What is the saturation point?
p: Model the production distribution of prompt and output lengths and arrival patterns, drive open-loop load in steps, record TTFT, inter-token latency percentiles, throughput and errors, and find the rate that still meets the SLO.
tip: Say the saturation point at the SLO is the number you report.

q: How do you compare two models for a task fairly?
a: I control everything except the model. Use the same evaluation set, the same prompt where sensible, and separately tuned prompts where each model deserves its best effort, and report both. Fix the sampling parameters, and for stochastic settings run multiple samples and average, with confidence intervals so I can tell real differences from noise. Grade with the same rubric or judge, blind to which model produced the answer, and use pairwise comparisons with randomised order for subjective tasks. Slice the results by category, difficulty and input length to see where each model is better, because the overall average hides trade-offs. Compare the total picture: quality, latency, throughput, cost per task, context limits, safety behaviour, licensing, data residency and operational complexity. Finally, validate the winner in a shadow or canary deployment, since public leaderboards rarely match your own data and constraints.
f: Why report both shared and tuned prompts?
How do you know a difference is significant?
p: Same evaluation set, controlled parameters, multiple samples with confidence intervals, blind grading, results sliced by category, and a full comparison of cost, latency, safety and licensing. Confirm in shadow or canary.
tip: Say your own evaluation beats public leaderboards for decisions.

q: How do you test for bias and fairness in an AI system?
a: I begin by defining the context: who is affected, which groups matter, what a harmful outcome looks like, and which fairness notion is appropriate, such as equal error rates or equal opportunity across groups, because different definitions can conflict. Then I build evaluation data that includes relevant slices, either from labelled attributes where it is lawful and appropriate, or from counterfactual tests, where I change only a name, gender or dialect in an otherwise identical input and check whether the output changes. I measure performance and error rates per slice, and for generative models test for stereotyping, toxicity and differences in tone or refusal across groups. Findings guide mitigations: better data, prompt and policy changes, post-processing, or restricting the use case. I document the results in a model card, monitor in production, and involve legal and domain experts, since fairness is a socio-technical question, not only a metric.
f: What is a counterfactual test?
Why can fairness definitions conflict?
p: Define affected groups and the fairness notion, test per-slice error rates and counterfactual variants, check generative outputs for stereotyping and refusal differences, mitigate, document in a model card, monitor, and involve legal and domain experts.
tip: Say fairness is socio-technical, not only a metric.

q: What is regression testing for prompts and models, and how do you automate it in CI?
a: Because changing a prompt or switching a model can break behaviours that previously worked, I keep a regression suite of cases that must continue to pass. It includes golden examples with expected outputs or assertions, past bugs, safety cases, format checks and cost and latency limits. In CI, a change to a prompt, tool definition, retrieval configuration or model version triggers the suite: the system runs against the cases, assertions check deterministic properties like valid JSON, required fields, forbidden content and tool call correctness, and a judge scores subjective quality against a rubric. Results are compared with the baseline stored from the main branch, and the pull request fails if quality drops beyond a tolerance or cost rises sharply. To manage cost and flakiness, I use a small fast subset on every commit and the full suite nightly, set low temperature or multiple samples, and cache results where inputs are unchanged.
f: How do you handle flaky LLM tests?
What is a tolerance threshold?
p: Maintain golden cases, past bugs and safety cases; on any prompt, tool, retrieval or model change run assertions and judge scoring against the main-branch baseline, failing on quality drops or cost spikes. Use a fast subset per commit and full runs nightly.
tip: Say you compare against a stored baseline with a tolerance.

q: How do you measure and reduce hallucinations in a customer-facing assistant?
a: I define hallucination operationally: statements not supported by the provided sources or by verified facts. I measure it with a test set of questions that includes answerable ones, unanswerable ones where the correct behaviour is to say it does not know, and traps that tempt the model to invent details. For RAG systems, I compute faithfulness by checking each claim against the retrieved context using a judge or an entailment model, and I sample production answers for human review. Reduction strategies work in layers: better retrieval, instructions that require citations and allow uncertainty, shorter and cleaner context, low temperature, constrained output formats, tool use for facts such as order status, and post-generation verification that removes or flags unsupported claims. For high-stakes topics, I add human review or restrict the assistant to approved answers. I track the rate over time as a key metric, and alert on increases.
f: Why include unanswerable questions in the test set?
How do you verify claims automatically?
p: Define hallucination as unsupported claims, measure with answerable, unanswerable and trap questions plus faithfulness scoring and human sampling, and reduce it with better retrieval, citations, I-don't-know behaviour, tools, verification and human review for high stakes.
tip: Say unanswerable test questions measure honesty.
